opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest signal is when it's clear the person has done something concrete before reaching out. I get a lot of emails that boil down to "I'm interested in mech interp, can you mentor me?" Totally understandable, but it gives me nothing to go on. Contrast that with "I read your paper on X, I tried replicating the result on a slightly different model, here's a short write-up and a notebook, and I noticed this weird thing in layer 3 that I can't explain." That person has shown me they can take initiative, actually write code, and engage with the details.

A few other things matter too. Brevity is a big one. If the email is five paragraphs of background before getting to the point, I'm probably going to skim it or miss it entirely. A good cold email respects that the recipient is busy: a couple of sentences on who you are, the concrete thing you did, and a specific, easy-to-answer ask. "Would you be willing to look at this two-page write-up and tell me if the direction seems promising?" is much easier to say yes to than "Can we hop on a call sometime?"

I also really value calibration and honesty about uncertainty. If someone says "I think I found X, but I'm not confident, and here's the sanity check I ran," that reads as much more competent to me than someone overclaiming. Research taste is a lot about knowing what you don't know, and you can see glimmers of that even in a short email.

And finally, it shouldn't feel like a template. If I can tell the same email went to twenty researchers with the name swapped out, it's not very compelling. Whereas if it's clear you've engaged with my work specifically, even briefly, that goes a long way. The bar isn't that high, frankly. Most cold emails don't do these things, so doing even a couple of them well makes you stand out.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the honest answer is that most cold emails I get fail within the first two sentences, and the ones that succeed are usually doing something quite simple: they show me evidence rather than telling me about themselves.

The failure mode is something like, "Hi Neel, I'm really passionate about AI safety, I've read a lot of your work, I'd love to chat and get your advice on getting into interpretability." And I don't doubt the person is sincere! But that email contains zero information I can use to distinguish them from the hundred other people who sent me the same thing. Passion is cheap to claim. Having read my stuff is cheap to claim. And "get your advice" is asking me to do all the work of figuring out what they actually need.

What signals competence is when someone has already done something. The best cold emails I've gotten are basically: "I spent two weeks trying to reproduce result X from your paper. Here's a short writeup. I got the main thing to work but I'm confused about Y, and I think Z might actually be going on — am I wrong?" That's incredibly legible. I can see in thirty seconds that they can code, they can read a paper carefully, they're willing to put in unglamorous effort before asking for anything, and they have the beginnings of research taste because they noticed something confusing and had a hypothesis about it. Even if the hypothesis is wrong, that's fine — being wrong in a specific, falsifiable way is a sign of a real thinker.

A few other things. Concision matters a lot — if you can't compress your point, I take that as weak evidence you don't understand it. Specificity matters: a concrete question I can answer in two minutes is vastly more likely to get a reply than an open-ended "can we have a call." And linking to artifacts — a GitHub repo, a blog post, a Colab notebook — is enormously stronger than describing the artifact, because it lets me check for myself.

And one thing I'd push back on, because I think people get this wrong: you don't need to have done something impressive. The reproduction doesn't need to be novel. The writeup can be rough. What I'm looking for is evidence that you're the kind of person who, when left alone with a problem, actually makes progress on it rather than waiting for permission. That's by far the most important trait in a junior researcher, and it's almost impossible to fake in an email, which is exactly why it's such a good signal.

astra-6.text:
I think the strongest signal is that you’ve actually done something, and you can explain clearly what you did and why it matters. There’s a big difference between “I’m really interested in your research, can we chat?” and “I read this paper, I was confused by this result, so I ran this experiment. Here’s what I found, and here’s the bit I’m still confused about.” The second gives me something concrete to engage with.

And it doesn’t have to be some incredible result. A small, thoughtful experiment can show that you’re able to take initiative, think carefully, and notice when the evidence doesn’t support your original idea. I’d much rather see that than a lot of impressive-sounding language.

Also, make the ask clear and easy to answer. If I can understand what you’ve done and what you want from me in a couple of paragraphs, that helps a lot.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is evidence that you’ve actually thought about the problem. It’s very easy to write, “I’m really interested in mechanistic interpretability. Can we chat?” And that doesn’t give me much to go on. Whereas if you say, “I read this post of yours, I tried this experiment, here’s what happened, and here’s the specific thing I’m confused about,” that’s much more compelling.

It doesn’t have to be some amazing research result. Even a small project can show that you can take initiative, engage with something technical, and notice when you don’t understand it. And a clear, specific question makes it much easier for me to give a useful response. You’ve done some of the work of figuring out what the conversation should be about.
